issues.legal_issue: A share of ancestral property allotted to a male coparcener on partition remains coparcenary property in relation to his male descendants, giving them an interest in it.
material_facts: An ancestor and his sons partitioned ancestral property, and one son received the property at issue.
That son had sons and a grandson, who brought the suit challenging a later transfer of the property.
issues.conclusion: The property allotted to the son retained its coparcenary character as regards his male descendants, who had an interest in it; the suit was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Mitakshara law, property inherited from a father or other specified paternal ancestor is ancestral, and a coparcener’s share of ancestral property remains ancestral as regards his male issue. The Court relied on C. Krishna Prasad v. C.I.T., Bangalore, M. Yogendra v. Leelamma N., and Rohit Chauhan v. Surinder Singh.

predicates.ancestral_family_partition_dispute: Family members disputed rights in property treated as ancestral and divided by partition.
predicates.share_derived_from_ancestral_property: A male family member received a share of the ancestral property in the partition.
predicates.male_descendants_of_allottee_exist: The allottee had male descendants who claimed an interest in the property.

issues.definition: When a family partition dispute concerns an allotment derived from ancestral property and the allottee has male descendants, those descendants have a coparcenary interest in the allotment.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument that transfers immovable property through an exchange cannot be admitted to prove that transfer.
material_facts: Two parties executed an exchange instrument concerning their respective properties.
The instrument’s terms included a building, and the building’s value exceeded the registration threshold described by the Court.
The instrument was not registered, and one party argued that the exchange concerned only businesses.
issues.conclusion: The instrument was inadmissible to the extent it purported to transfer the immovable property; it could not be proved by the document or by oral evidence as proof of its contents.
issues.legal_principle: Section 118 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines exchange and requires a transfer completing an exchange to follow the mode applicable to a sale; Sections 54 of that Act and 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 require registration for the transfer at issue. Section 49 of the Registration Act bars an unregistered document required to be registered from affecting the immovable property or being received as evidence of the transaction. The Court relied on Roshan Singh v. Zile Singh and Section 91 of the Evidence Act, 1872 concerning proof of the contents of a document.

rule.if: civil_property_transfer_dispute and exchange_instrument_covers_immovable_property and property_value_requires_registration and instrument_unregistered

predicates.civil_property_transfer_dispute: A civil dispute concerned the purported transfer of property between parties.
predicates.exchange_instrument_covers_immovable_pro: The parties’ exchange instrument included a transfer of immovable property.
predicates.property_value_requires_registration: The value of the immovable property was such that the transfer had to be made by a registered instrument.
predicates.instrument_unregistered: The instrument used to record the exchange was not registered.

issues.definition: In a civil property-transfer dispute, an unregistered exchange instrument covering immovable property that requires registration is inadmissible to prove the transfer of that property.

issues.legal_issue: A party seeking protection for possession in part performance must plead that the possession was taken in part performance of the contract.
material_facts: A party relied on an agreement and asserted that possession was protected because the agreement had been acted upon.
That party’s written statement did not plead that possession had been taken in part performance of the contract.
issues.conclusion: The party could not claim the benefit of protection for possession in part performance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires a party seeking its benefit to plead that possession was taken in part performance of the contract. Pleadings give notice of each side’s case and identify the matters for decision; relief cannot be granted without the necessary pleading.

predicates.property_dispute_involving_part_performa: A property dispute involved a party relying on an agreement as a defense based on part performance.
predicates.party_seeks_part_performance_protection: A party asked the court to protect possession on the basis that the agreement had been acted upon.
predicates.possession_in_part_performance_not_plead: The party’s pleadings did not state that possession had been taken in part performance of the agreement.

issues.definition: When a party in a property dispute seeks protection based on part performance but does not plead that possession was taken in part performance, that protection is unavailable.
